"I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed." Anyone who enters upon a science must know its definition and its principles. The definition of this science is: the knowledge by which the meanings of the speech of Allah are known. Its name is the science of tafsīr.

Tafsīr and taʾwīl are not one and the same in meaning. Tafsīr means the explanation of the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, from the perspective of what has been transmitted (al-manqūl). Taʾwīl means confirming what the text can sustain of meaning from the perspective of reason (al-ʿaql). Transmitted reports are indispensable in tafsīr, for the Qurʾān says to the Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s.: "so that you might make clear to the people what has been sent down to them" (Q. 16:44). For this reason tafsīr relies upon what the Messenger explained. When no transmitted report from the Messenger is found, tafsīr by rational inference is accepted, because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: "an Arabic Qurʾān, so that perhaps you might reason" (Q. 43:3). This verse has given us the right to exercise reason in order to understand the meanings of the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

ʿAlī, r.a., was asked: "Do you possess a book that the Messenger of Allah singled out for the People of the House?" He replied: "No, only the Book of Allah, or an understanding of it that Allah grants to a Muslim man." And ʿAlī, r.a., said: "The Qurʾān is supple, possessed of many aspects; accept its aspects." Whoever holds fast to something that has an aspect in the Qurʾān, let none dispute it with him.[1]

Both tafsīr and taʾwīl must rest upon transmission or reason. The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., forbade interpreting the Qurʾān by mere personal opinion. The interpretation of the Qurʾān requires knowledge of Arabic speech, knowledge of the legal rulings, knowledge of rhetoric and literary craft, and a light in the heart of the interpreter.[2]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[1] Ibn Saʿd transmits via ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib sent him to the Khārijites with the instruction: 'Go to them and dispute with them, but do not use the Qurʾān as your evidence against them, for it is possessed of many aspects (dhū wujūh); dispute with them through the Sunna.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya likewise observes that great numbers of the pious predecessors interpreted the Qurʾān freely from their understanding, and that they entrusted this to the Muslim community.

[2] The prohibition of interpreting the Qurʾān by mere ungrounded opinion (tafsīr bi-l-raʾy al-mujarrad) is widely transmitted. Al-Suyūṭī enumerates fifteen sciences required of the Qurʾānic commentator in his al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, among them Arabic linguistics, morphology, rhetoric, principles of jurisprudence, occasions of revelation, and the science of sound transmission (ʿilm al-riwāya). The distinction between blameworthy opinion and praiseworthy rational inference (ijtihād) is discussed at length in that work.

This Book was sent down to us by Allah as guidance and light, unlike all other books. Whoever holds fast to it arrives at what he seeks; whoever neglects it goes astray. It is the word of the Lord of all existence, revealed in the language of the Arabs, the most eloquent of all languages. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: "Verily We have revealed it as an Arabic Qurʾān so that you might reason" (Q. 12:2). It is reported from the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s.: "The superiority of the speech of Allah over all other speech is like the superiority of Allah over His creation." Whoever recites it and acts by it is like a citron: its taste is good and its scent is good; and whoever hears it and acts not by it is like the date: its taste is good but it has no scent.

The science of tafsīr is the noblest of all sciences, because the nobility of any science is measured by the nobility of its subject-matter, and the subject of this science is the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. No speech is nobler than the speech of Allah; therefore no science is nobler than the science of tafsīr. Any science that requires the science of tafsīr is itself a subordinate science, for the Qurʾān is the foundation upon which every other Islamic science rests: ḥadīth, fiqh, kalām, and taṣawwuf all return to it for their authority and validity.

The commentator of the Qurʾān occupies the highest station among the scholars, because he speaks about the meaning of the speech of Allah. This station entails a corresponding obligation: he must know the Arabic language in its depth and breadth, and he must possess sound understanding so that he does not carry the speech of Allah to a meaning it cannot bear.

The wisdom in beginning the recitation of the Qurʾān with the words of seeking refuge (al-istiʿādha) is that the reciter is about to engage with the word of Allah, which is the greatest of all speech. Satan desires to distract him from understanding it, to cast doubt into his heart, or to cause him to stumble in its recitation. By saying "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed," the reciter places himself under the protection of Allah, who drives Satan away from him so that he may receive the divine speech with a pure heart and attentive mind.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, commands this at Q. 16:98: "When you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed." The word rajīm (accursed) comes from the root r-j-m, meaning to stone and drive away. Satan is named rajīm because he was cast out and banished from the mercy of Allah.

A student once went repeatedly to a scholar in Khurāsān until he had memorized four thousand ḥadīths from him. He said: "I shall go to the other scholars and debate with them, for I have become learned." He came to a gathering of scholars and began to speak; they refuted him on every point, until he felt ashamed and returned to his teacher. He said: "Master, I memorized four thousand ḥadīths from you, yet the scholars refuted me at every turn." The scholar replied: "Go and learn, for the knowledge of ḥadīth is not the same as the knowledge of the religion. Knowing a narration is not understanding it." The student returned and continued to study, and he became one of the scholars.

This story illustrates that tafsīr requires not only the memorization of transmitted material but deep understanding, sound reasoning, and God-given insight. A person may memorize the words of scholars and yet remain ignorant of their meanings.

The Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s., once came out to the mosque and encountered two groups of people. In one group, people were engaged in supplication and remembrance of Allah. In the other, people were engaged in learning and teaching. He said: "Both groups are engaged in good. As for this group: they supplicate to Allah, and if He wills He grants them, and if He wills He withholds. As for this group: they learn and teach the ignorant. I was sent as a teacher." And he sat with the group that was learning and teaching.

The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., is thus the supreme teacher, and the knowledge he taught is the foundation. Among the most important aspects of this knowledge is the knowledge of the Book of Allah, its words, meanings, and the sciences surrounding it. To sit in a circle of learning is therefore to follow the practice of the Prophet.
"By Allāh's Name, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful."

The scholars differed extensively over the basmala and its status: whether it is an independent verse of Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, or a verse revealed at the head of every sūra but not of the Fātiḥa specifically, or a separator between sūras with no independent verse-status of its own. The scholars of Qurʾānic recitation differ: the Medinans, led by Nāfiʿ, hold that it is not a verse of the Fātiḥa; the Kūfans, led by ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī, hold that it is.[3]

What is established without dispute is that the basmala was revealed as part of the Qurʾān. Its revelation marked the beginning of every sūra, and the Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s., knew the conclusion of one sūra and the beginning of the next by the descent of the basmala. The Prophet never began any affair of consequence without saying it, and the believer is instructed to begin every righteous act with it so as to seek the blessing (baraka) of Allah's name.[5]

The basmala comprises nineteen letters, and the guardians of Hell who attend the Fire are nineteen in number (Q. 74:30). The scholars of tafsīr note the correspondence: whoever takes refuge in the basmala with true sincerity may hope for protection from each of the nineteen.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[3] Transmitted by Abū Dāwūd with a sound chain from Ibn ʿAbbās: 'The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not know the boundary between two sūras until Bismi llāhi l-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm was revealed to him.' See Sunan Abī Dāwūd, Kitāb al-Ṣalāh. Al-Qurṭubī transmits the same point at the relevant location in his commentary.

[5] Transmitted via Wāqiʿ from al-Aʿmash from Abū Wāʾil from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd: 'Whoever wishes Allah to protect him from the nineteen guardians of Hell, let him recite Bismi llāhi l-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm, so that Allah may make for each of its letters a shield against each one of them.' The nineteen guardians are mentioned in Q. 74:30: 'Over it are nineteen.'

"I recite in the name of Allah" or "we recite in the name of Allah": a person begins and does not say "I begin" (abtadiʾu), because "beginning" can be understood in a material sense, whereas reciting is a spiritual act from the outset. The bāʾ here is for accompaniment (mulābasa): it indicates that the recitation is performed while being accompanied by, or grounded in, the name of Allah.[4]

The name Allāh is the greatest and most comprehensive of the divine names. It is the name that the Qurʾān ascribes to the Being who possesses all perfection; all the other names (al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Malik, and the rest) are attributes that qualify it. The name Allāh is not shared by any created being; no child has ever been named Allāh, nor has any idol. It is therefore the most particular and the most sublime of the names of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

Al-Raḥmān (the Compassionate) and al-Raḥīm (the Merciful) are both derived from the root r-ḥ-m (mercy). Al-Raḥmān denotes an intense, encompassing mercy that extends over all creation in this world, believers and disbelievers alike. Al-Raḥīm denotes a mercy that is reserved for the believers specifically in the hereafter. This is why the Qurʾān says: "And He is ever Merciful (raḥīm) to the believers" (Q. 33:43): the specific mercy of the raḥīm is for the people of faith.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[4] Ibn Jazī al-Kalbī, al-Tashīl li-ʿUlūm al-Tanzīl: 'Allāh is a primitive proper noun (ism murtajal jāmid); the alif and lām in it are constitutive of the name itself, not the definite article. The view that it is derived from al-taʾalluh (absolute devotion/worship) is also transmitted.' Ibn Kathīr further reports that al-Rāzī preferred the view that the name is not derived at all, citing al-Khalīl, Sībawayhi, and the majority of the uṣūliyyūn and jurists.

The basmala contains nineteen letters, and the guardians of the Fire are nineteen (Q. 74:30). There is a transmitted tradition that whoever recites the basmala sincerely, Allah will make for him from each of its letters a shield against one of the nineteen guardians.

The basmala is also required at the opening of the prayer. No prayer is valid for one who does not recite Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, and no recitation of the Fātiḥa is complete without its opening: "By Allāh's Name, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful." The scholars debate whether it is recited aloud or silently in the prayer, and the practice varies among the established schools of law. What is agreed upon is that it is recited.
Meccan, seven verses.

This sūra is Meccan because the prayer was instituted in Mecca, and the prayer requires its recitation; Allah would not institute the prayer without providing the sūra to be recited in it. It is the opening of the Book (fātiḥat al-kitāb): fātiḥa means "the opening" or "that which opens." Allah opened His Book with it because it contains a summary of the entire Qurʾān: the praise of Allah, the affirmation of the divine attributes, the acknowledgment of servitude, and the supplication for guidance.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[8] Among the traditions cited in support of the Fātiḥa's excellence: the narration transmitted by Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal in his Musnad from ʿAbdullāh ibn Jābir; and the narration in the Musnad Abī Dharr recorded in the Jāmiʿ al-Kabīr, in which Abū Dharr asked: 'O Messenger of Allah, how many books (kutub) did Allah send down?' He replied: 'One hundred and four books, of which thirty are in al-Fātiḥa.'

In a sacred ḥadīth transmitted by Muslim, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My slave in two halves, and My slave shall have what he asks for." When the slave says al-Ḥamdu li-llāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn, Allah says: "My slave has praised Me." When he says al-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm, Allah says: "My slave has extolled Me." When he says Māliki yawm al-dīn, Allah says: "My slave has glorified Me — and has submitted himself to Me." When he says Iyyāka naʿbudu wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn, Allah says: "This is between Myself and My slave, and My slave shall have what he asks for." When he says Ihdina l-ṣirāṭa l-mustaqīm to the end, Allah says: "This is for My slave, and My slave shall have what he asks for."[6]

This is the greatest honor a slave can receive: that Allah personally responds to each verse of the prayer with words of acceptance and acknowledgment. No other act of worship carries this direct divine dialogue in the same form.[7]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[6] Al-Tirmidhī transmits from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Al-Ḥamdu li-llāh [i.e., Sūrat al-Fātiḥa] is the Mother of the Qurʾān (umm al-Qurʾān), the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb), and the Seven Oft-Repeated Verses (al-sabʿ al-mathānī).' Cf. Q. 15:87: 'We have given you seven of the oft-repeated and the mighty Qurʾān.'

[7] Transmitted by Muslim from Abū Hurayra in a sacred hadith (ḥadīth qudsī): 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant in two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks for. When the servant says al-Ḥamdu li-llāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn, Allah says: My servant has praised Me (ḥamidanī ʿabdī). When he says al-Raḥmāni l-Raḥīm, Allah says: My servant has extolled Me (athnanī ʿalayya ʿabdī). When he says Māliki yawm al-dīn, Allah says: My servant has glorified Me (majjadanī ʿabdī)...' See Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Kitāb al-Ṣalāh.
"al-ḥamdu lillāh (The Praise is for God), Lord of all the worlds."

Al-ḥamd (praise) covers every expression of gratitude and commendation that exists. Every act of praise and thanksgiving that any created being has ever offered belongs either to its description or to its consequence. The categories of ḥamd are divided according to whether it pertains to Allah's attributes or to His acts. The attributes of Allah are eternal and unacquired; His acts in the world are the grounds for the gratitude of His creatures.

The al at the opening of al-ḥamd indicates totality (istighrāq): all praise, of every kind, from every creature, in every time, belongs to Allah alone, Blessed and Exalted. Praise offered to other than Allah is ultimately grounded in His bounty, since all beauty, goodness, and perfection in creation are reflections of His attributes.
"You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help."

The shift from third-person in the earlier verses ("Lord of all the worlds," "the Compassionate, the Merciful," "Master of the Day of Judgment") to second-person address here is a figure of speech called iltifāt (turning): the worshipper has praised Allah and drawn near to Him through that praise, and now turns to address Him directly, as one who has arrived in the presence of the Beloved.

Iyyāka naʿbudu (You alone we worship): worship (ʿibāda) in the complete sense is the submission of the whole self to Allah, encompassing all outward acts and inward states. Wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn (and from You alone we seek help): the slave acknowledges that he is incapable of worship, or of any good, without the enabling grace of Allah. He places worship before seeking help, because the act of worship establishes the relationship; the petition for help flows from the relationship.
"Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray."

The "straight path" (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) is the path of Islam in its completeness: creed, practice, ethics, and purification. It is "straight" because it leads directly to Allah without deviation. The slave asks for guidance to this path in every prayer, in every rakʿa, because guidance is not a single event but a continuous divine gift that must be renewed at every moment.

Those "upon whom You have bestowed favor" are those who believed in what lay beyond their perception (al-ghayb). The ghayb has two kinds: what is hidden from you but known to others, and what is absolutely hidden from all created beings and known only to Allah. The believer accepts both kinds with full conviction based on the testimony of the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s.

The four attributes mentioned at the opening of the sūra for the believers — taqwā, faith in the unseen (al-ghayb), establishment of prayer (iqāmat al-ṣalāh), and spending in charity (al-infāq) — correspond, in the exegetical tradition, to the four rightly guided caliphs. Taqwā corresponds to Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, who excelled in God-consciousness above all. Faith in the unseen corresponds to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who accepted what was reported to him without hesitation. The establishment of prayer corresponds to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, who was known for his all-night prayers. And spending in charity corresponds to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, about whom, according to the tradition, Q. 2:274 was revealed: "Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly."[9]

In this reading, the opening of Sūrat al-Baqara speaks not only of the general community of believers but of the particular excellences of the four who led that community after the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s. Each caliph embodied in the highest degree one of the four qualities that define the God-fearing. Their example is thus inscribed at the very threshold of the longest sūra in the Qurʾān, as an invitation to the believers of every age to follow in their footsteps.

"I seek refuge in Allāh from Satan the accursed. By Allāh's Name, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful."

O Allah, bestow blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the opener of what had been closed and the seal of what had preceded, the helper of truth through truth, the guide to Your straight path, and upon his family, the true measure of his worth and his immense station. May Allah be pleased with the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ṣ.a.w.s.

Having described the elect among His slaves with those qualities and mentioned their ultimate destination, He followed this with the description of His enemies. He dedicated four verses to the characteristics of the believers, two verses to the disbelievers, and thirteen verses to the hypocrites.

Kufr (disbelief) linguistically means covering and concealing. In the terminology of Islamic law, it signifies the denial of something whose arrival from the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., is necessarily known. Al-kāfir (the disbeliever) appears in the Qurʾān in four categories: (1) the disbeliever as the opposite of the believer, as in "Verily those who disbelieve and hinder from the path of Allah" (Q. 4:167); (2) the disbeliever in the sense of one who denies, as in "whoever rejects it — Allah is Self-Sufficient, above all the worlds" (Q. 3:97), meaning whoever denies the obligation of ḥajj; (3) the disbeliever as the opposite of the grateful, as in "Give thanks to Me and do not disbelieve" (Q. 2:152); and (4) the disbeliever in the sense of one who disavows, as in "then on the Day of Resurrection you will disavow one another and curse one another" (Q. 29:25), meaning you will disavow one another.[1]

The varieties of kufr are as follows. The kufr of the knowing denier: one who knows the existence of the True, Blessed and Exalted, and yet denies Him by tongue, as in the kufr of Iblīs and the kufr of the Jews: "and when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it" (Q. 2:89). The kufr of absolute negation: denying the existence of the Creator entirely, as with most disbelievers. The kufr of one who knows the truth inwardly but does not profess it by tongue and does not practice the religion, as occurred with Abū Ṭālib, who said in verse: "Verily I know that the religion of Muḥammad / is among the best of all the religions of mankind." He uttered this with his tongue and believed it in his heart, yet he did not enter Islām and thus died a disbeliever. And the kufr of hypocrisy (al-nifāq): professing belief by tongue while denying it in the heart.

Kufr, as we established, is the denial of something whose arrival from the Prophet Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., is necessarily known: the oneness of Allah, Blessed and Exalted; the performance of prayers; fasting Ramaḍān; the obligatory nature of zakāh on wealth; ḥajj; and the Resurrection. Whatever is necessarily known to have come from the Prophet, its denial is kufr. As for what cannot be known to have come from the Prophet except through careful investigation and discernment, one who denies it does not become a disbeliever. The distinguishing marks which the scholars have enumerated as acts of kufr — such as wearing the zunnār (the monk's belt) and the ghiyār — are signs of kufr, not kufr in themselves. Whoever is seen wearing the zunnār is declared with certainty to be no believer, because the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., forbade it; yet it carries no self-gratification the way fornication or wine-drinking do. Those are forbidden by the Law, but they contain pleasure for the lower self, and whoever commits them is not a disbeliever because the self overcame him through desire. But wearing the zunnār carries no pleasure whatsoever: whoever wears it has contemptuously dismissed the Islamic religion, and he is a disbeliever. Anyone who meets Allah, Blessed and Exalted, bearing any form of kufr will dwell forever in the Fire: "Verily Allah does not forgive that anything be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills" (Q. 4:48).

(Verily those who disbelieve) — that is, people such as Abū Jahl, Abū Lahab, and those like them among the disbelievers — (it is equal to them whether you warn them or you do not warn them: they will not believe), because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, knew this of them; so do not aspire to their faith.

The True, Blessed and Exalted, informed His Prophet that these disbelievers would never believe. He did not say "it is equal to you whether you warn them or not," for warning and leaving warning are not equal concerning the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., since he is obligated to convey the message. If he conveys it, whether anyone believes or not, he is rewarded. But as for the disbelievers who will not believe: warning and not warning them are equal to them, for they will never believe. Allah informed His Prophet of this in advance so as to cut off his hope for their faith, so that he might not suffer as Nūḥ suffered. After spending one thousand minus fifty years among his people, Allah revealed to him: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed" (Q. 11:36). After enduring those tribulations, Allah informed him. But the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., was told in advance, so that he would not long for their faith. And when Nūḥ came to know that his people would not believe, he called down destruction upon them; but the Prophet, upon learning that his people would not believe, did not call down destruction upon them, for he is the Prophet of Mercy: "We did not send you save as a mercy to all the worlds" (Q. 21:107).

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, established in this verse that warning them and not warning them are equal. The disbelievers themselves acknowledged this regarding their prophet Hūd: "It is equal to us whether you admonish us or are not among those who admonish" (Q. 26:136). And in the hereafter, when they are cast into the Fire, they will be told: "Bear it patiently or do not — it is the same for you" (Q. 52:16). Just as Allah declared it equal for them in this world regarding warning, so they are made to know in the Fire that their patience and their impatience are alike. And they themselves say: "Whether we are distressed or patient, it is the same for us: there is no way out for us" (Q. 14:21).

(Allah has set a seal on their hearts), stamped upon them and locked them so that no good enters them, (and on their hearing), so they are unable to benefit from the truth they hear, (and on their eyes is a covering), so they cannot see the truth. (And for them is a mighty punishment): a powerful and eternal chastisement, which is the Fire. "Mighty" (ʿaẓīm) is the opposite of paltry, just as "great" (kabīr) is the opposite of small, and ʿaẓīm surpasses kabīr in degree. This punishment is exceedingly severe, severer than every other punishment. This concerns the disbelievers.

And this was revealed concerning the hypocrites, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and his companions, who when they came to the Muslims said to them "We are with you," and when they went to the disbelievers said "We are with you."

(And among the people are those who say: "We believe in Allah and in the Last Day"), that is, the Day of Resurrection, called "the Last Day" because it is the final of all days, (yet they are not believers). The plural form is used in accordance with the sense of "those among the people." (They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe), by displaying outwardly the opposite of what they conceal inwardly of disbelief, so as to ward off from themselves the worldly consequences of kufr. (Yet they deceive none but themselves): because the harm of their deception returns to them. They are exposed in this world through Allah's informing His Prophet of what they concealed, and they will be punished in the hereafter. (And they do not perceive it.)

As for the grammatical note: yukhādiʿūna here is a form of the pattern fāʿala, which normally denotes mutuality between two parties, but here it applies to one party alone, just as one might say in Arabic "I punished the thief" or "I treated the patient," using fāʿala without a partner. The mention of Allah in "they seek to deceive Allah" is an elevation of the Muslims' station, for in truth they are only deceiving the believers; but Allah made the deception of the Muslims equivalent to deceiving Him, Blessed and Exalted.

(In their hearts is a disease), that is, doubt and hypocrisy, which ail their hearts. (So Allah increased their disease) through what He sent down of the Qurʾān, because they rejected it. This disease may be understood as spiritual: the doubt and hypocrisy in their hearts is a moral sickness. Or it may be understood as a genuine physical pain, because the continuous and ever-increasing strength of the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., and the growing might of the Muslims caused them anguish until it became as though a bodily disease. (And for them is a painful punishment), a torment that causes pain, (because they used to lie) — in the reading of Ḥafṣ — or "because they used to disbelieve" in the reading of Warsh.[2]

[2] The reading kadhhabū ('they used to lie') is that of the majority transmission, including the reading of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim. The variant kafarū ('they used to disbelieve') is the reading transmitted via Warsh from Nāfiʿ, which is the primary reading of North and West Africa. Both readings are canonical (mutawātir) and carry independent exegetical weight; the Warsh variant sharpens the alignment of the verse with the preceding descriptions of unbelief.

(And when it is said to them), these hypocrites, ("Do not spread corruption in the earth"), through disbelief and diverting people from faith, (they say: "We are only reformers"), claiming that what they do is not corruption but rather merely maintaining relations with both sides and serving their own interests. But in truth they are only corrupters. Allah declared: (Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters — but they do not perceive it). Alā is a particle of alertness. "Innahum hum al-mufsidūn" carries double emphasis. But the triple emphasis with the lām of affirmation is absent, because they do not actively perceive their own corruption; they genuinely believe themselves to be reformers.

A philosopher once posed a question to a scholar: "We see redundancy in Arabic speech — people say 'Zayd is standing,' then 'Indeed Zayd is standing,' then 'Indeed Zayd is certainly standing.' Is this not mere padding?" The Arab scholar replied: "'Zayd is standing' is a straightforward declaration of Zayd's standing. 'Indeed Zayd is standing' is an answer to an implied question. 'Indeed Zayd is certainly standing' is a refutation of someone who denies it." The hypocrites said "We believe" using a verbal form (āmannā), a lighter and less committed expression. Allah replied to them: "They are not believers," using the nominal form with the negation of mā, which is stronger, for it expels them entirely from the totality of believers. Had He said only "they did not believe," that alone would not have removed them from the community of believers.

(And when they meet those who believe, they say: "We believe"), using the verbal form: lighter in expression. But when they returned (to their satans), their chiefs and leaders, (they say: "We are with you"), using the nominal form with inna, a stronger assertion of loyalty. ("We were only mocking") them by displaying belief. (Allah mocks them), requiting them for their mockery. (And He extends them in their transgression), giving them respite in their exceeding of all bounds through kufr, (wandering blindly). (Those are they who purchased error in exchange for guidance): they took misguidance in place of guidance. (So their trade brought no profit, and they were not guided) in what they did.

Then Allah struck two parables for the hypocrites, for a parable affords the clearest possible illustration: it represents what is absent through what is present, and what is conceptual through what is sensory. (Their likeness), their condition in their hypocrisy, (is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire), one who lit a fire in darkness. (When it illumined all around him), when he could see and had found warmth and protection from what he feared, (Allah took away their light), extinguishing it. He did not say "took away their fire" because the purpose in kindling a fire is the light it produces. (And He left them in darknesses unable to see), confused and confounded about the way, fearful. Just so, these hypocrites believed by uttering the word of faith; when they die, fear and punishment come upon them. (Deaf): they are deaf to the truth and do not hear it with a hearing of acceptance. (Dumb): mute in goodness and unable to utter it. (Blind): to the path of guidance and unable to see it. (They will not return) from misguidance.

(Or like a rainstorm from the sky), or their likeness is as those beneath a rain shower, (in which are darknesses): the darkness of night, the darkness of heavy cloud, and the darkness of falling rain. (And thunder), the angel charged with the rain, or its sound. (And lightning), its flash. (They put their fingers into their ears against the thunderbolts, fearing death) from hearing it. Just so, these hypocrites: when the Qurʾān descended containing the mention of kufr, likened to darkness, and threats against it, likened to thunder, and its clear proofs, likened to lightning, they stopped their ears so as not to hear it, lest they be moved to believe in what they heard that they desired, and lest they be held to what they loathed. This is the parable of the hypocrites.[3]

The hypocrite is a disbeliever at heart; yet seeing the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., bearing a sword, killing those who opposed him and seizing their wealth, he came and pronounced the two testimonies of faith: "There is no god but Allah; Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah," though he was not sincere in his heart. He prayed with the Muslims and gave charity. By this he protected himself and his wealth in life. But death is inevitable; and when he dies, he enters a punishment far more severe than what he had feared in life.

(Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing), meaning their ears, (and their sight. Verily Allah is over all things powerful), including the taking of what has been mentioned.

The Qurʾān has now established the descriptions of the believers, the disbelievers, and the hypocrites. The Qurʾān began with the "clear" (muḥkam), Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, a perfectly composed sūra, and followed with Sūrat al-Baqara, the first verse of which is "ambiguous" (mutashābih): "Alif. Lām. Mīm." These letters are the weightiest thing for the Arabs, because they understood nothing of what these letters contain. The Qurʾān, in its miraculous nature, is recognized through its eloquence, its rhetorical excellence, and its knowledge of the unseen. The Arabs understood everything that appeared in the Qurʾān until these letters appeared at the openings of certain sūras, and they could discern not the faintest trace of their meaning. These letters are the hardest thing upon them.

Every Arabic word drawn from the roots of the language carries a meaning that matches the nature of the root. For example, the root k-l-m carries in the Arabic language the meaning of force and intensity. This meaning appears in all its derivations: the kalima (word) is so called because it strikes the hearing and the mind of a person until he grasps its meaning; kalam in another sense is the grievous wound, a severe strike. Every word of the Arabs has a derivation and variations. The kalima appears in the Qurʾān in the sense of ʿĪsā, who is called "a word" because he came into being from the command "kun" (Be!), without the agency of a father. And in the usage of the Arabs, they call a full ode a kalima and a sermon a kalima. The Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s., said: "The truest word the poet ever uttered is the word of Labīd: 'Truly, everything besides Allah is vanishing.'" Yet these disconnected letters: the Arabs found in them no trace of meaning. They are therefore the greatest miracle for the Arabs, surpassing all the other miracles of the Qurʾān.[4][5]

When the first of the disconnected letters, "Kāf. Hā. Yā. ʿAyn. Ṣād.," was revealed, Jibrīl would normally recite the whole verse to the end and then explain it, and the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., would repeat it as Jibrīl had recited it and explain it as well. But when Jibrīl brought the revelation "Kāf," the Prophet said: "I understand." "Hāʾ" — "I understand." "Yāʾ" — "I understand." "ʿAyn" — "I understand." "Ṣād" — "I understand." The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., knew their meanings before Jibrīl knew them. Jibrīl thereby came to know that this is a secret concealed even from him, the very one charged with conveying the revelation.[6]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[4] The epithet kalima (word) applied to ʿĪsā ibn Maryam is discussed in detail by al-Suyūṭī and al-Maḥallī in Tafsīr al-Jalālayn on Q. 3:45: 'His name is the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Mary, eminent in this world and the next, and of those brought near.' They explain that he is called 'a word from Him' because he came into existence through the divine command kun (Be!), without the agency of a father, unlike all other created beings. Ibn Kathīr transmits the same explanation in his commentary on Q. 3:39.

[5] Al-Bukhārī transmits in his Ṣaḥīḥ (no. 6147) from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'The truest word the poet ever uttered is the word of Labīd: Alā kull shayʾin mā khalā llāha bāṭilu — Truly, everything besides Allah is vanishing.' Muslim transmits the same hadith (no. 4187). Labīd ibn Rabīʿa al-ʿĀmirī was a celebrated pre-Islamic poet who subsequently embraced Islām and ceased composing poetry.

[6] The tradition of Jibrīl pausing at each disconnected letter while the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, responded 'I understand' (fahimtu) at each one, establishing that the Prophet possessed foreknowledge of their meaning before the angel himself had disclosed it, is cited by al-Bursawī in Rūḥ al-Bayān, vol. 28, p. 166, in the context of the opening letters of Sūrat Maryam (Kāf. Hā. Yāʾ. ʿAyn. Ṣād.). The tradition underscores the distinction between prophetic knowledge (ʿilm ladunnī) and angelic knowledge of transmitted revelation.

The Sheikh, r.a., describes the believers and adorns them with the finest qualities: taqwā (God-consciousness), faith in the unseen (al-ghayb), the establishment of prayer (iqāmat al-ṣalāh), and spending from what Allah has provided them.

Prayer is mentioned by Allah in the Qurʾān in a number of verses: "Establish the prayer" (aqīmū al-ṣalāh), meaning not merely to perform a prayer but to establish it, to erect it and perfect it and correct it in every aspect so that it contains no deficiency. Allah commanded the performance of prayer in congregation: "and bow with those who bow" (Q. 2:43). And He commanded that it be performed with full inward submission: "those who are humble in their prayers" (Q. 23:2).

The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., and those who followed him, may Allah make us and you among them, fulfilled all of these commands entirely: they established the prayer, performed it in congregation and in its proper time, and humbled themselves within it. Allah mentioned them and mentioned their final destination: "Those are the inheritors who shall inherit al-Firdaws; therein they shall abide" (Q. 23:10-11).

He also mentioned those who stand in contrast: those who "belied and turned away" (Q. 75:32) and their recompense: "What has brought you into Saqar? They said: 'We were not among those who prayed'" (Q. 74:42-43). And those who came after and neglected prayer: "Then there followed after them a generation who wasted the prayer and followed desires; they shall encounter perdition" (Q. 19:59). Whenever Allah mentions prayer, He joins it with zakāh, because prayer is the greatest act of bodily worship and spending in charity is the greatest act of worship with wealth; and no one's religion is complete unless he worships with both his body and his wealth.
Having described the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and the believers, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, then called all of humanity to His oneness, which is the greatest of all things.

(O Mankind), the people of Mecca and all who surround them from throughout the world, (worship), that is, unify, (your Lord who created you), who brought you into existence when you were nothing, (and those before you), and who created those before you, (so that perhaps you might be God-conscious): laʿalla in the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, carries the force of certainty and confirmation. But from the perspective of the slave: Allah commands him to worship and to unify his Lord, yet the slave must not feel safe but must rather hope and fear. Thus "perhaps you might be God-conscious" requires no reinterpretation; the slave hopes to be among the muttaqīn and fears that he may not attain it.

He then explains the rationale for singling out Allah alone for worship: (He who made the earth a resting place for you), a spread-out expanse upon which to recline, not so hard that nothing can find rest upon it nor so soft that nothing can stand upon it. Allah made it firm yet yielding so that you may settle upon it standing, seated, or lying down. (And the sky a canopy): He who raised this roof above us. (And sent down from the sky water): the rain descends first from the sky, then reaches the clouds, then descends from the clouds to the earth. (By it He brought forth all kinds of fruits as provision for you), which you eat and with which you feed your animals. (So do not set up rivals to Allah), partners in worship, (while you know): do not worship other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted, while you know that He alone is the Creator. If a person knows that Allah is the Creator, he knows that none deserves his worship except Allah.

Among those of the deluded: one who knows that Allah created him yet does not worship Him; one who knows that Allah provides for him yet does not rely upon Him; one who knows this world passes away yet clings to it; one who knows his heirs will be his adversaries yet gathers wealth for them; one who knows death is coming yet has not prepared for it; one who knows with certainty the grave is his dwelling yet has not prepared it; one who knows with certainty the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ) is his crossing yet has not lightened his load; one who knows with certainty the Fire is the abode of the wicked yet has not fled from it; one who knows with certainty Paradise is the dwelling of the beloved of Allah yet does not seek it; and one who knows with certainty that Iblīs is his enemy yet does not do battle with him.[7]

The categories of shirk (associating partners with Allah) are three: the manifest shirk, that practiced by the polytheists in the worship of idols; the hidden shirk, acting for the sake of reputation and public praise; and the most hidden shirk, perceiving anything other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

It is narrated that Allah has charged seven angels with the deeds of the slave. If he performs an act, the angels carry it upward; the angel of the lowest heaven examines it and says: "Return this deed upon its owner — he is a slanderer" or "a backbiter." In each successive heaven, deeds of arrogance, self-admiration, jealousy, ostentation, and love of fame are similarly returned. If a deed passes through all the heavens, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: "This person concealed from you what lies within him; but nothing is concealed from Me. This deed was not intended for My face — return it upon its owner, for he intended other than Me." For this reason it is narrated from the Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s.: "People are destroyed save the believers; the believers are destroyed save the scholars; the scholars are destroyed save those who act; those who act are destroyed save the sincere; and the sincere are in a state of peril."[8]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[7] The enumeration of 'ten of the deluded' (ʿasharat al-maghbūnīn) is a well-known didactic tradition in Sufi and ethical literature. Al-Ṣāwī cites a version of it in his Ḥāshiyat al-Ṣāwī ʿalā Tafsīr al-Jalālayn in the context of Q. 2:22, as an elaboration on the verse's call to worship Allah alone. The tradition appears in various forms across the classical literature of akhlāq and waʿẓ (homiletics), attributed to different early authorities.

[8] The tradition of the seven angels charged with the servant's deeds, each in successive heavens examining and returning deeds tainted by slander, backbiting, arrogance, self-admiration, jealousy, ostentation, and love of fame, is widely circulated in the literature of tazkiyat al-nafs (spiritual purification). The report concludes with Allah's refusal even of a deed that passed through all seven heavens but was not sincerely intended for His face alone. The tradition is cited in various forms by al-Ghazālī in Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn and by later commentators on sincerity (ikhlāṣ).

(And if you are in doubt about what We sent down to Our slave), that is, the Prophet Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., as to whether it is truly from Allah, (then bring a sūra like it): meet the challenge of the Qurʾān. Bring one sūra comparable to it in eloquence, beauty of composition, and knowledge of the unseen. The shortest sūra is Sūrat al-Kawthar, comprising three verses. (And call your witnesses), your gods whom you worship, (besides Allah, if you are truthful) in claiming that Muḥammad composed it himself. If you can do so, then do — for you are Arabs, eloquent and fluent like him.

The Qurʾān first challenged with the whole Qurʾān itself: "Say: if all of mankind and the jinn were to gather to produce the like of this Qurʾān, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to one another supporters" (Q. 17:88). Then it challenged them with ten sūras: "Then bring ten invented sūras like it" (Q. 11:13). Then it challenged them with a single sūra, even the size of "We have surely given you al-Kawthar" — and they were unable. The Arabs, with all their eloquence and rhetorical mastery, did not come forward to compete with the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., in producing the like of the Qurʾān. The only one who dared was Musaylama the Arch-Liar, and Allah so disfigured his attempt that his words sounded as though they were not those of an Arab at all. His imitation of Sūrat al-Kawthar was: "We have given you jewels; pray to your Lord and make yourself manifest." What connection is there between jewels and prayer? Jewels are something of the adornments of this world, far removed from "We have surely given you al-Kawthar; so pray to your Lord and sacrifice."[9]

The Americans once commissioned a man learned in Arabic to compose something like Sūrat al-Fātiḥa. He said: "In the name of the Lord of all existence," abandoning the name Allāh, which is indispensable in speaking of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and saying instead "Lord of all existence" (rabb al-akwān), abandoning "all the worlds" (al-ʿālamīn) for a modern coinage not found in classical Arabic. He then said "Yours is the worship and in You I seek help," intending to condense "You alone we worship and from You alone we seek help" (iyyāka naʿbudu wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn) into four words; but he turned al-mustaʿān into a verbal noun, distorting the grammar entirely. Anyone who hears these words knows immediately that they are not the speech of a native Arab, that the speaker has never mastered classical Arabic.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[9] Musaylama ibn Ḥabīb al-Ḥanafī, known as 'the Arch-Liar' (al-Kadhdhāb), was a claimant to prophethood in the Arabian Peninsula during and after the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His attempt to imitate Sūrat al-Kawthar, widely quoted by Muslim scholars as evidence of the Qurʾān's inimitability (iʿjāz), is cited in various tafsīr works including Ibn Kathīr's commentary and al-Suyūṭī's al-Itqān, chapter on the taḥaddī. He was killed at the Battle of Yamāma (12 AH / 633 CE) during the Ridda Wars.

(But if you do not do it — and you will never do it), if you are unable to produce what was asked of you, because you are incapable, and you never will be, (then fear) Allah through faith. (The Fire whose fuel is people), the disbelievers, (and stones), their idols which they had worshipped, (prepared for the disbelievers): it has been made ready for them; they will all be punished therein together.

(And give glad tidings to those who believe), who have affirmed faith in Allah, (and do righteous deeds), from the obligatory acts and the supererogatory acts, (that for them are gardens), orchards with trees and dwellings, (beneath which rivers flow): beneath their trees and their palaces flow the waters. The waters pour forth in Paradise without limit and without machinery; they flow with the inhabitants wherever they are needed.

(Every time they are given provision from its fruits, they say: "This is what we were given before" — and they are brought resemblance thereof): they are offered provision from the fruits of Paradise and say that this resembles what they received before. (And for them therein are purified spouses), purified from menstruation and from every impurity. (And therein they shall abide), dwelling there forever, neither dying nor ever departing from it.[10]

O Allah, bestow blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the opener of what had been closed and the seal of what had preceded, the helper of truth through truth, the guide to Your straight path, and upon his family, the true measure of his worth and his immense station.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[10] The tradition concerning the least of the people of Paradise receiving 'eight thousand previously married women (thayyibāt) and four thousand virgins (abkār) and one hundred ḥūrīs' is transmitted in several hadith collections in varying formulations. Al-Qurṭubī discusses such traditions in his commentary on Q. 2:25 (al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, vol. 1), noting that the ḥūrīs (al-ḥūr al-ʿīn) are described in the Qurʾān as purified spouses (azwāj muṭahhara) and as companions of equal age (atrāb). See also the relevant discussions in Ibn Kathīr's commentary on Q. 44:54 and Q. 56:22-23.

إِذْ جَرَقْنَا  ·  بِكُمُ الْبَحْرَ فَأَنجَيْنَٰكُمْ  ·  وَأَغْرَفْنَا عَالَ مِرْعَوْنَ  ·  وَأَنتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسِىّ أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً  ·  مِنْ بَعْدِو  ·  وَأَنتُمْ ظَلِمُونَ  ·  ثُمَّ عَبَوْنَا عَنكُم  ·  بَلاء  ·  عظيم من ربكم
مِنْ بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونٌ وَإِذَ اتَيْنَا مُوسَى الْكِتَبَ وَالْمُرْفَاتَ
لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونُ وَإِذْ قَالَ مُوسِىٰ لِقَوْمِهِ، يَقَوْمٍ إِنَّكُمْ ظَلَمْتُمْ وَ أَنْجُسَكَم بِائِخَاذِكُمْ الْعِجْلَ  ·  دَلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ عِنْدَ بَارِبِكُمْ  ·  قَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْوَ

كُلُواْ مِن طَيَّبَاتِ مَا رَزَّفْتَٰكُمْ  ·  وَمَا ظَلَمُونَا وَلَكِ كَانُوَا أَنْجُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ  ·  وَادْخُلُوا أَلْبَابَ  ·  سُجَّدا  ·  يُعْبَرْ لَكُمْ خَطَيْكُمْ وَسَتَزِيدُ الْمُحْسِنِينُ بَبَدَّلَ الذِينَ ظَلَمُوا  ·  فَوْلًا غَيْرَ ألذِى فِيلَ لَهُمْ  ·  «أَنزَلْنَا عَلَى ألذِيرَ ظَلَمُوا رِجْزان عذابا طاعونا مِ السَّمَآءٍ بِمَا كَانُوا يَمْسُفُونَ
"I seek refuge in Allāh from Satan the accursed. By Allāh's Name, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful."

O Allah, bestow blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the opener of what had been closed and the seal of what had preceded, the helper of truth through truth, the guide to Your straight path, and upon his family, the true measure of his worth and his immense station. May Allah be pleased with the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ṣ.a.w.s. There is no power and no strength except in Allah, the Most High, the Tremendous.
O aspiration (himma) of the Shaykh, draw near to us at this gathering; incline toward us with a glance that shall bring us to triumph.

(Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a similitude — even that of a gnat or what is above it.) This verse was revealed in response to what the Jews said when Allah struck the similitude of the fly, in His saying (And if the fly should rob them of anything, they could not rescue it from it), and the similitude of the spider in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt, in His saying (like the spider). They said: What did Allah intend by mentioning these lowly things? It is not fitting that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, should strike similitudes with such contemptible things — it was His due to be ashamed of that. So the verse was revealed. This is the occasion of the revelation of this verse: Allah struck a similitude with these contemptible things, and the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and the Jews found it objectionable that a similitude of this kind should be struck concerning the Majestic, Blessed and Exalted. So Allah responded to them, saying (Indeed Allah is not ashamed) — that is, He does not refrain — (to strike) — to make — (a similitude, even that of a gnat or what is above it). Allah is not ashamed to give a similitude by means of the gnat, or by something lesser than it, or by something above it; He does not omit to make clear the wisdom contained therein. (As for those who believe, they know that it) — the similitude — (is the truth), established and situated exactly where it belongs,

(from their Lord). When a similitude of this kind is struck, people fall into two categories: the believers know that the similitude is situated exactly where it belongs; (but as for those who disbelieve, they say, What did Allah intend by this as a similitude?) — that is, by this similitude? He answers: (thereby He leads many) — by this similitude — (astray) from the truth, on account of their disbelief, (and thereby He guides many) of the believers, on account of their affirmation of it, (and thereby He leads astray none but the wicked transgressors).

He is not ashamed to strike a similitude. Shame (istiḥyāʾ) is the constriction a servant feels when doing something for which he would be reproached or blamed, such that he abandons it. This constriction, arising from aversion to being blamed, is impossible in respect of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. We stated to you as a principle that every attribute impossible of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, if you examine it closely, you will find has a beginning and an end: its beginning is impossible in respect of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, while its end is permissible in respect of Him. Shame is the constriction felt before a thing for which one would be blamed or reproached, such that one abandons it; the abandoning is the end-point, and abandonment is indeed permissible of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Since a person of great standing is restrained from doing a given thing only by shame — for he fears no one, so nothing checks him but shame — and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is greater than every great one, the term shame has been applied to Him in a figurative sense, the intended meaning being simply abandonment: that is, He does not abandon striking the similitude out of any shame.

The disbelievers who objected to the striking of a similitude with these contemptible things did so out of their obtuseness and the blindness of their hearts. For these contemptible things are among the strangest of what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has created, and they contain wonders found in nothing else. The gnat, for instance, despite the smallness of its body, possesses every organ found in the elephant, and two wings besides. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, who had the power to create the elephant, also had the power to create the gnat and to fit into it organs and joints equal in number to those of the elephant; nothing is beyond His power. This small creature, the mosquito — when Allah created it weak, and likewise created the fly weak — He placed in it such boldness that it fears no one. When people gather, you find the fly hovering over their eyelids and their eyes, and however vigorously they drive it away, it returns to them, unconcerned; even kings, even tyrants, the mosquito alights upon them without fearing them.

As for the elephant and the lion, Allah created them at the utmost degree of strength and solidity, yet He placed within them such timidity that they do not dare draw near to people; they dwell in the wilderness, and if they hear the sound of a human being, they flee from him. This is among the subtle kindnesses (luṭf) of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: had He placed this boldness and daring found in contemptible creatures within these powerful ones, they would have harmed people, indeed destroyed them within a short time. Had the lion dared approach a human being as the fly and the mosquito dare, all people would have perished. But out of His kindness, Blessed and Exalted, He placed fear in the strong and boldness in the weak, which harms no one. Yet the fly, when it lands on you, spoils your life for you, whether you are in your house or your garden or wherever you may be; and the mosquito is likewise. Given the contemptibility, weakness, and helplessness of these creatures, how then can one dare to defy Allah, Blessed and Exalted, given the severity of His punishment and what is in Hellfire of scorpions and serpents whose harm is unceasing? Everyone who disobeys the command of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and abandons what He has commanded, is like one who dares this severe punishment, while a mere flea or mosquito or fly is enough to spoil his life and trouble him. Let him know, then, that he cannot bear anything of the punishment of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

And despite their contemptibility, these things do not prevent the similitude from being exactly fitting: (O mankind, a similitude has been struck, so listen to it: those you call upon besides Allah will never create a fly) — this is of the utmost eloquence. And He struck a similitude for the worship of idols: (their likeness is as the likeness of the spider that takes to itself a house, and truly the frailest of houses is the house of the spider). The striking of similitudes with such things also occurred in the scriptures revealed before the Qurʾān.

Al-Maʾmūn was once upon his pulpit when a fly landed on him; he drove it away, and it landed on him again repeatedly, and however he drove it away he could do nothing to prevent it. So he sent for Abū Hudhayl, a scholar in the city, to ask him what wisdom lay in Allah's creation of these things. Abū Hudhayl said to him: Allah created these things to humble tyrants such as yourself, for when the tyrannical king sits upon his throne, the fly lands upon his excrement and then lands upon him, and he is powerless to keep it away. Al-Maʾmūn said to him: You have spoken truly; it is for this that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, created it.

It is said, too, that were it not for the winds and the flies, the world would putrefy — for these foul odors are consumed by the flies, and the winds carry them away so that they dissipate; were it not for that, the world would putrefy and harm its inhabitants. He said, (thereby He leads many astray and thereby He guides many). How can He, Glorified is His Majesty, say that He guides many, when the people of guidance are few in relation to the people of misguidance? The people of misguidance are many and the people of guidance are few; yet despite their fewness, they are many in themselves — not in relation to the people of misguidance, but many in themselves. Or: the people of truth, even if few, are the vast majority in weight, the many, the prevailing ones, and it is by them that the standard is set. But in reality, those who go astray are more numerous than those who are guided, and this is due to the rarity of true faith and to Allah's utter independence of His creation, Blessed and Exalted — had He willed, He would have caused everyone on earth, all together, to believe: (And had your Lord willed, everyone on earth, all together, would have believed). But because of His independence from creation, He made most of the jinn and mankind people of misguidance. (And thereby He leads astray none but the wicked transgressors) —

those who go outside obedience to Him — (those who break the covenant of Allah), that which He entrusted to them in the scriptures concerning belief in Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s. Allah's covenant is threefold: the first is that which He took from the progeny of Adam on the day He said, (Am I not your Lord?) and they said, (Yes indeed); the second is that which He took from the prophets, that if they should live to see the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., they would believe in him and follow him; and the third is that which He took from the scholars: (You shall make it clear to mankind and not conceal it). This covenant the Jews broke. He described the covenant as broken as though He had made it a rope, for the covenant is called a rope in the speech of the Arabs, and this is why it is permissible to speak of its being broken. (after its solemn confirmation) — after its being made firm — (and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined), namely belief in the Prophet, the bonds of kinship, and other things, (and work corruption in the earth), through acts of disobedience and obstruction of belief — (those are the losers), because of their destiny to the Fire made everlasting upon them.

(How can you disbelieve) — O people of Mecca — (in Allah, when you were) — indeed you were — (dead), mere sperm-drops within the loins, (and He gave you life) — in the wombs, in this world, by breathing the spirit into you — the interrogative here expresses astonishment: how can they disbelieve after all this? Not at all! (Then He shall cause you to die), when your appointed terms come to an end, (then He shall give you life), through resurrection, (then to Him you shall be returned) — you shall be brought back after the resurrection, and He will requite you for your deeds.

And He offered a proof of the resurrection, since they denied it: (It is He who created for you all that is in the earth) — the earth and everything in it — (altogether), that you might benefit from it and take heed. The Truth, Blessed and Exalted, informed us that He created the earth and everything in it for the children of Adam, all of it, so that they might benefit from it and take heed that the Creator who has the power to do this has the power to resurrect them after their death. Here the lām indicates entitlement — that is, it was the children of Adam who came to possess the earth and what is in it — it does not indicate unrestricted permissibility. This is the error into which the Ibāḥiyya fell, a doctrine among the doctrines of the Muʿtazila, who say that Allah created everything in the earth for the children of Adam, so that nothing on the face of the earth is forbidden to us once Allah has created it for us. But this is not what is intended.

(Then He turned) — after creating the earth, He directed His purpose — (to the heaven and levelled them), that is, He made them — (seven heavens, and He has knowledge of all things), knowing everything, in its totality and in its detail. Do you not then take heed that the One who has the power to create this in the first instance, which is far greater than you, has the power to bring you back again? In this verse, (He created for you all that is in the earth, altogether; then He turned to the heaven), it seems that the creation of the heaven came after the creation of the earth, whereas in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt it is said, (and the earth, after that, He spread out), which seems to indicate that the creation of the earth came after that of the heavens. The reconciliation between the two is that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, created the earth first, then created the heavens, and after creating the heavens, He spread out the earth and made it as it is now — so each of the two is, in a sense, both prior and posterior to the other.

And, mention, O Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., (when your Lord said to the angels, Indeed I am placing a vicegerent (khalīfa) on the earth) — one who will succeed Me in carrying out My rulings therein. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, related that He informed the angels that He was placing a vicegerent on earth, and this was Adam. (They said, Will You place therein one who will work corruption therein) — through acts of disobedience — (and shed blood) — spill it through killing, just as the sons of the jinn had done, for they existed before Adam and used to work corruption in the earth and shed blood — will You place a vicegerent like them? (While we glorify You with praise) — engaged in praising You, saying, Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him — (and sanctify You), declaring You exalted above whatever does not befit You. (He said, Indeed I know what you do not know) — of the benefit contained in making Adam a vicegerent, and that among his progeny would be both the obedient and the disobedient, so that justice would become manifest among them. And they had said: our Lord will never create a creature more honored in His sight than us, nor more knowing, since we preceded him and have seen what he has not seen. So Allah, exalted is He, created Adam from the surface of the earth — that is, its face — taking a handful from all its various colors, which was kneaded with different waters, then fashioned him and breathed into him the spirit, so that he became a sentient living being after having been inanimate matter. This is the story of Adam's vicegerency.

Allah said, (Indeed I am placing a vicegerent on the earth) — this is Adam. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, made him His vicegerent in existence, through whom all His rulings and works are carried out — like the seal by which every king safeguards his kingdom. And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, mentioned that when He created Adam, He created him as a human being; when He spoke of him as a human being, He said, (Indeed I am creating a human being), whereas here, when speaking of him and making him a vicegerent, He said placing, not creating — for in his capacity as vicegerent, he does not belong to the created realm (ʿālam al-khalq) but rather to the realm of command (ʿālam al-amr).

He informed the angels that Adam and his progeny would be Allah's vicegerents on earth, and the angels responded with this reply, (Will You place therein one who will work corruption therein and shed blood?) From where did they know that the progeny of Adam would work corruption in the earth and shed blood? They knew it from the very constitution of Adam's creation. Allah created Adam and placed within him a soul possessed of desire (shahwa) and anger (ghaḍab), and also reason (ʿaql). The human being has three faculties: the faculty of anger, which sheds blood; the faculty of desire, which works corruption in the earth through sins; and the faculty of reason, which sets things right. So the angels looked at Adam and said that these two faculties would inevitably overpower the single remaining faculty, and thus corruption and bloodshed would inevitably occur.

It is also said that they understood that Adam and his progeny would work corruption in the earth from the very word vicegerency (khilāfa) itself, for khilāfa is derived from khilāf, meaning contravention — every vicegerent must inevitably contravene the one before him. Since Adam was to be Allah's vicegerent, they understood that corruption and bloodshed would necessarily proceed from him. Or, they read this in the Preserved Tablet, for it was written there that Adam would be a vicegerent on earth and would have progeny, some of whom would work corruption in the earth and shed blood until Allah filled Hell with them, and some of whom would be obedient, and Allah would fill Paradise with them; they read this in the heavenly books, and this is why they said what they said. Or, they had heard this from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, previously, when He addressed them privately beforehand, and they said to Him: O our God, this Fire is a creation of tremendous power — what will You do with it? He said to them: I shall create a creature and bring forth progeny from his loins; among them will be those who obey Me, and I shall admit them into Paradise, and among them will be those who disobey Me, and I shall admit them into the Fire. Their objection to Adam's vicegerency, then, they understood from these various considerations.

(While we glorify You with praise and sanctify You. He said, Indeed I know what you do not know.) So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, turned away from them, (and He taught Adam the names) — the names of the things named, that is, the names of all created beings — (all of them), down to the large bowl and the small bowl, the small emission of wind and its diminutive, and the ladle. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, taught him everything that He would create: this one's name is horse, and the wisdom in it is such-and-such; this one's name is donkey, and this... down to the large bowl and the small bowl, the large vessel and the small one, and the ladle — Adam came to know every single thing at once, from the beginning of time to its end, while the angels knew nothing of this.

(Then He presented them to the angels and said), in reproach, (Inform Me) — tell Me — (of the names of these), the things named, (if you speak truly) — that is, in claiming that I would not create anyone more knowing than you, or that you are more deserving of the vicegerency than Adam. (They said, Glory be to You!) — declaring You exalted above any objection to You — (we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise), from whose knowledge and wisdom nothing escapes.

(He), exalted is He, (said, Adam, inform them) — the angels — (of their names), the things named. Adam named every single thing by its name and mentioned the wisdom for which it had been created. (And when he had informed them of their names, He), exalted is He, (said to them), in rebuke, (Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you disclose) — what you revealed in your saying, Will You place therein... — (and what you were concealing) — what you were keeping secret, namely your saying that Allah would never create anyone more honored in His sight than you, nor more knowing.

This is the story of Adam with the angels. When Allah created Adam, He taught him these things, which the angels did not know, and so Allah argued against them that Adam deserved the vicegerency because he possessed knowledge which the angels did not possess. This is why the scholars have said that leadership (imāma) is deserved only by the one who possesses knowledge — for Allah, Blessed and Exalted, argued against the angels concerning Adam's vicegerency by means of knowledge. This is the merit of knowledge (ʿilm). Because Adam knew the names of things and the angels did not know them, Allah made him a vicegerent on earth and commanded the angels — as will shortly be related — to prostrate to him in a prostration of greeting. This is proof of the nobility of knowledge: knowledge is the leader, and action follows it. The merit of knowledge is established by the Book, the Sunna, and reason.

As for the Book, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, mentioned the merit of knowledge in a number of verses, among them: (It is only those of His servants who possess knowledge that truly fear Allah), and among them: (Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels, and those possessed of knowledge). And Allah mentioned four categories of people whose ranks He raises: the people of Badr — (The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble), this having been revealed concerning the people of Badr, and He said at the end that He raises their ranks, granting them lofty degrees; and He mentioned those who strive (mujāhidūn) — (Allah has preferred those who strive above those who sit back, by a tremendous reward, by degrees); and He raised, Blessed and Exalted, the ranks of the righteous — (and whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds — those shall have the highest ranks); and He raised the ranks of the people of knowledge above all of these categories — (Allah raises those of you who believe, and those who have been given knowledge, in ranks) — placing those possessed of knowledge in the third rank: (Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels, and those possessed of knowledge).

In the Qurʾān there are seven individuals of whom Allah mentions that He taught them knowledge directly from Himself, without intermediary: (He taught Adam the names, all of them), and by this he attained the vicegerency and the prostration of the angels to him; and He, exalted is He, said that He taught al-Khiḍr the knowledge of insight (firāsa): (and We had taught him knowledge from Our presence), and by this he gained a disciple like Moses and Joshua; and He taught Joseph the interpretation of dreams: (My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty and taught me the interpretation of narratives), and by this he attained Zulaykhā and the kingdom; and He taught David the craft of making coats of mail: (and We taught him the making of coats of mail), and by this he attained leadership and kingship; and He taught Solomon the speech of birds: (we have been taught the speech of birds) — and the Teacher was Allah — and by this he attained the kingdom, and Bilqīs, and the Throne; and He taught Jesus the Book, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel: (and He will teach him the Book, wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel), and by this he attained being raised up to heaven and fellowship with the angels; and He taught Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., the sacred law: (and He taught you what you did not know), and by his knowledge he attained the power of intercession.

ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his countenance, said: Knowledge is superior to wealth in seven respects:
– Wealth is the inheritance of the Pharaohs, while knowledge is the inheritance of the prophets.
– Wealth diminishes through spending, while knowledge does not diminish through spending.
– Wealth is possessed by the disbeliever and the believer alike, while knowledge is possessed only by a believer.
– Wealth requires a guardian and a protector, while knowledge protects its possessor and requires no protector.
– When a person dies, his wealth remains behind, but his knowledge enters the grave together with him and does not leave him.
– Wealth weighs a person down on the Bridge (ṣirāṭ), while knowledge strengthens him to walk upon the Bridge.
– All people are in need of knowledge for the sake of their religion, but they are not in need of the possessor of wealth.

O Kumayl, knowledge is better than wealth: knowledge guards you, while you must guard wealth; knowledge governs, while wealth is governed; wealth is diminished by spending, while knowledge grows through being expended.

Knowledge, then, is superior to wealth. And if Adam, upon him be peace, was taught the names of created things, and was ennobled by that knowledge to the point that he received the prostration and greeting of the angels, then we have been taught the Essence, the Attributes, and the Names — not the names of created things, but rather the Names of Allah, His Attributes, and His exalted Essence. Once we know this, how could we fail to attain the greeting of the angels? Indeed, we attain something beyond that: the greeting of the Lord Himself — (Peace! — a word from a Merciful Lord). And if al-Khiḍr, through the knowledge of insight, attained the companionship of Moses and Joshua, two prophets, then we, having attained the knowledge of ultimate reality (ʿilm al-ḥaqīqa), how could we fail to attain the companionship of Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s.? We do attain it: (those are with the ones whom Allah has favored, of the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous — and excellent are those as companions). Praise be to Allah.

Among the merits of knowledge is that when the student leaves his house for a scholar in pursuit of knowledge, the angels spread their wings for him in honor and veneration; and as long as he continues going to his teacher, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sends mercy down upon him; and while he is in a gathering of knowledge, the one who understands the knowledge knows what benefit he attains, while the one who understands nothing of what is said still attains blessings — he attains the fact that he is in obedience to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, as long as he remains in the gathering of knowledge, even if he understands nothing; he is thereby restrained from sins and transgressions as long as he remains in that gathering, and he sits in the company of scholars and angels. And if he understands nothing of what is said, his heart is humbled on that account, and so Allah becomes his companion: (I am with those whose hearts are humbled for My sake). This is something of the merit of knowledge.
When Allah wished to alert the angels that Adam was better than them, He gave him of knowledge what they did not possess, and so they acknowledged that Adam was better than them.

And, mention, O Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., (when We said to the angels, Prostrate to Adam) — a prostration of greeting, involving a bow, or as though it were a bow of salutation, not a prostration of worship, which is due to none but Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Or, Adam was made a direction (qibla) for them, just as the Kaʿba was made a direction for us: we prostrate toward it, not to it in reality. In any case, this prostration to other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has been abrogated. (So they prostrated, except Iblīs) — he is the father of the jinn, who was among the angels — (he refused), declining to prostrate, (and was proud), saying, I am better than he, (and he became one of the disbelievers). Iblīs used to be called ʿAzāzīl; he was a servant brought near to Allah, having worshiped Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon every handspan of the face of the earth for a thousand years, and he had been treasurer of Paradise for forty thousand years, and had striven in worship for sixty thousand years — all of this before Adam. When Allah created Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate to him, Iblīs reasoned by analogy (qiyās) despite the presence of the explicit text, saying that he was better than Adam and so would not prostrate to him. He refused, while the angels prostrated.

The prostration was originally a single act, and this was what analogy required and what was fitting, since Allah is One, so the prostration was one. But when the angels had prostrated for half a day — five hundred years — and raised their heads from the prostration, and saw that Iblīs had refused and had not prostrated, they returned to prostration a second time, prostrating a second prostration in gratitude to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, that He had not tried them with what He had tried Iblīs. Thus the prostration became twofold: there was one bowing (rukūʿ) and one prostration (sujūd), because the One worshiped is one, but the second prostration was an act of thanksgiving to Allah, Blessed and Exalted.
وَإِذِ إسْتَسْفِى مُوسى اذكر يا محمد إذ استسقى، الإستسقاء طلب السقيا لِفَوْمِهِ،
